lesson.title: Volts, Amps, Watts, and Ohms: The Circuit's Unit System
lesson.summary: Every circuit quantity has a precisely defined SI unit built from more basic units, and keeping those units straight is what lets formulas like Ohm's law and the power law actually work out numerically.
lesson.body:
Voltage, current, resistance, and power are not just abstract symbols in a formula, each one carries a specific SI unit with a precise physical definition, and those definitions are what make circuit equations consistent. Current is measured in amperes, abbreviated A, and represents charge flowing past a point over time. Voltage is measured in volts, V, representing energy per unit charge, specifically one volt equals one joule per coulomb. Resistance is measured in ohms, using the Greek letter omega, and power is measured in watts, W, equal to one joule per second.

These units are not independent of each other, they are built from one another through the very laws you have already learned. Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, tells you that one volt equals one ampere times one ohm, which means an ohm can be defined as a volt divided by an ampere. Similarly, the power law, power equals voltage times current, tells you that a watt equals a volt times an ampere. You can even trace this back to energy and charge: since a volt is a joule per coulomb and an ampere is a coulomb per second, multiplying them gives joules per second, which is exactly a watt. The units check out because the physics is consistent.

In practice, circuit values rarely land on nice round numbers of ohms, volts, or amps, so engineers constantly use metric prefixes to keep numbers manageable. A resistor might be labeled in kilohms, thousands of ohms, using the prefix k, while a current might be measured in milliamps, thousandths of an amp, using the prefix m. Larger values use mega for millions, and smaller ones use micro for millionths. Converting between these prefixes correctly is just as important as knowing the underlying formula, because a decimal point in the wrong place turns a safe design into a smoking one.

Consider a 3.3 kilohm resistor, meaning 3.3 times 1000, or 3300 ohms, carrying a current of 2 milliamps, meaning 2 times 0.001, or 0.002 amps. Applying Ohm's law, voltage equals current times resistance, gives 0.002 amps times 3300 ohms, which equals 6.6 volts. Notice that the prefixes had to be converted to their base unit values, amps and ohms, before multiplying, mixing kilohms and milliamps directly without converting would give a wrong answer by orders of magnitude.

Getting comfortable moving fluidly between these units and their prefixes is a foundational skill for every calculation that follows in circuit analysis. Every law from here forward, current division, power dissipation, source transformation, assumes you can keep volts, amps, ohms, and watts straight, along with their kilo, milli, mega, and micro variations, without losing track of a decimal point.

One more habit worth building early is treating units as a built in error check on every formula you write. If a calculation that is supposed to produce a voltage instead leaves you with units of amp squared ohms per second, something has gone wrong in the algebra long before you look at whether the number itself seems reasonable, and catching that mismatch on paper is far cheaper than discovering it after building a circuit that does not behave as expected.
